description.narrative:
The aim with this intervention is to contribute to an increased number of South Sudanese children (particularly but not exclusively girls) whose life chances are transformed through education (impact). The outcomes of the program is an improvement in girls' educational attainment from that already achieved in GESS1; building further gains on school enrollment, reducing barriers to education and promoting equity in access for all children.
The outputs of the program are as follows: Output 1: Communication to girls, boys, women and men to shift attitudes and behavior related to the education of girls and children with disabilities. Output 2: Cash transfers to girls to improve enrollment, retention, transition and completion rates. Output 3: Capitation Grants to schools to improve learning environment for all learners. Output 3B: Strengthened Public Financial Management systems in the Ministry of General Education and Instruction (MoGEI) and improved policy formulation and implementation. Output 4: Quality of Education, Learning Groups & Resilience to contribute to improving learning outcomes. Output 5: Building a knowledge base for support to girls' education.

"Girls' Education South Sudan, Phase 2" (GESS2) is a five year program running from May 2019 to March 2024. Sida supports the final year of the program, April 2023-March 2024, with 18 MSEK. GESS2 is implemented in all ten states and three administrative areas of South Sudan, reaching around 4,000 not-for-profit, government, faith-based and community schools across the country. The total number of students paid under GESS2 until now is approximately one million girls. This is the second phase of the Girls Education South Sudan (GESS) program with the Foreign Commonwealth and Development Office (FCDO) as the Lead Donor and agreement partner. The program is also supported by Global Affairs Canada (GAC), the United State Agency for International Development (USAID) and the EU Delegation. The aim of GESS2 is to contribute to transforming life changes through education for South Sudanese children (particularly but not exclusively girls). The program provides a range of interventions - direct financial support to girls in form of cash transfers to support retention and completion; provision of capitation grants for flexible use by schools to support infrastructure, learning materials and access for children with disabilities; initiatives designed to improve the quality of education; research; support to girls through mentoring and learning groups; and large scale behavioral change interventions specific to the importance of girls' education. GESS2 has also included support to strengthen Public Financial Management in the Ministry of General Education and Instruction and the Ministry of Finance and Planning. In summary, The situation in the education sector in South Sudan clearly shows the importance of continued coordinated support from donors with a particular focus on the most vulnerable girls and boys in the country. By strengthening the capacity among students, teachers, schools, ministries at both state and national level through GESS2, a more sustainable education system is created.

"Girls' Education South Sudan, Phase 2" (GESS2) är ett femårigt program som pågår från maj 2019 till mars 2024. Sida stödjer programmets sista år, april 2023-mars 2024, med 18 MSEK. GESS2 implementeras i alla tio stater och tre administrativa områden i Sydsudan och når cirka 4 000 statliga, trosbaserade och kommunala skolor över hela landet. Det totala antalet elever som erhåller stöd genom GESS2 fram till nu är cirka en miljon flickor. Detta är den andra fasen av programmet Girls Education South Sudan (GESS) med Foreign Commonwealth and Development Office (FCDO) som huvudgivare och avtalspartner. Programmet stöds även av Global Affairs Canada (GAC), United Statens Agency for International Development (USAID) och EU-delegationen. Målet med GESS2 är att bidra till att en förbättring av livsvillkor för sydsudanesiska barn och unga (särskilt men inte enbart flickor) genom utbildning. Programmet innehåller en rad olika komponenter – kontantöverföringar som betalas ut till flickor, s.k. capitation grants till skolor, initiativ för att förbättra kvaliteten på utbildning, forskning och studier, stöd till flickor genom mentorskap och lärandegrupper, samt storskaliga satsningar för att förändra beteenden kopplade till flickors utbildning. GESS2 har också inkluderat stöd för att stärka den offentliga ekonomiska förvaltningen i utbildningsministeriet samt finans- och planeringsministeriet. Situationen inom utbildningssektorn i Sydsudan visar tydligt på vikten av ett fortsatt koordinerat stöd från givare, med ett särskilt fokus på de mest utsatta flickorna och pojkarna i landet. Genom att stärka elevers, lärares, skolors och ministeriernas kapacitet på både nationell och statlig nivå genom GESS2, kommer ett mer hållbart utbildningssystem att skapas.

title.narrative: Decision Girls' Education South Sudan Phase 2 (GESS2)

description.narrative:
Positive attitude towards girls education
Findings from the BBC endline survey conducted in September December 2023 indicate that the "Our School" radio program reached 2.8 million people aged 15 and above with information on the benefits of education to girls and children with disabilities. Regular listeners continue to demonstrate higher levels of knowledge about education and positive attitudes towards the education of girls and children with disabilities compared to non-listeners.
A successful distribution of cash transfers
The program has been successful in distributing CTs. The cumulative (first and second phase) of CT payments issued are 2,489,507. This is a few percent over the target that was set. In the second phase alone, 1,226,788 unique girls have received a GESS2 CT payment since the inception of the project's second phase. This represents 110% of the year 5 target. During the 2023 CT cycle, a total of 439,224 girls in 5,182 schools were validated in 2023 and eligible to receive the payment. Out of these, 427,534 girls in 5,153 schools were paid. Of these, 47,700 girls were candidates who received South Sudanese Pounds (SSP) 32,000, while 379,834 were noncandidates and received SSP 25,600.
Well planned activities and organisation
In addition, it should be noted that the consortium has been well organized and has planned its activities in a timely manner. This is showcased by the fact that funds have been consumed evenly. Each quarterly report provides information and updates on key performance indicators. In addition, it provides two stories of change illustrating the program's impact in practice. The annual report has infographics that provide easy access to relevant information regarding achievements.
Assessment of achieved results in relation to the objectives
Effective deliverance of cash transfers but causal linkages to school enrolment are unexplored
There is no doubt that the program has been effective in delivering cash transfers (CT) to female students. Although there has been a system in place in delivering the CT, there is little follow-up on knowing for what purpose the CTs have been used. During the second program phase between May 2019 to December 2023 around 1.2 million unique girls from primary 5 to senior 4 (ie students that are 11/12 years to 17/18 years of age) have received funds. It is, however, unclear of how much of these funds actually went to cover school costs. For example, the individual that was portrayed in the story of change for the reporting period April to June 2024 had reportedly given the cash to her mother so that she could develop her business which in turn would enable her eventually to pay the school fees one year later. Similar stories were echoed in the evaluation Some girls give the CT to their parents to pay for food or to pay into the School Development Fund, which is a fund for school fees paid by parents. The amount to be paid varies from school to school. p. 17. A teacher cited in the evaluation was reported saying: Girls are happy and the parents are happy too. We tell the girls not to give the money to their parents, but perhaps they give them money for food. They are suffering. Or they give money to a little brother or sister. We don't know. (p. 117) One can assume that the importance of the support was not only its monetary value, but also the sense of importance of attending school and motivation that the grant helped to foster. As one teacher in connection to the examination 2022/2023 at a secondary school in Nauru said Girls are performing better than the boys because of their harder working and commitments. The motivation is because of their needs being met. (p. 107).
The general assumption is that CT greatly helped improving girls attendance at schools. This assumption is echoed in the different narrative reports and evaluation. Although this might be the case, the casual linkage between CT and school attendance is circumstantial and an anecdotal level and not validated in the reporting. In addition, it would have been interesting to learn more on the social consequences of the CT and if and in that case how it influenced relations between social groups. Furthermore, the reason for exclusively choosing girls can also be questioned, as boys also live in poverty. This method may inadvertently deepen the gender divide. Applying a do no harm perspective would have enhanced the reporting.
Cash transfer not adjusted for inflation
As previously stated the program has been able to distribute CTs to 1.2 million girls during the second program phase. This is an impressive number that requires sophisticated program management. However, the value of these CTs was not adjusted for inflation. It has been stated in the reporting that at the end of the program period, the value of the CT had decreased considerable. At the end, it was reported that it was barely enough to cover the cost for a school bag. It raises questions as to why the financial management of the grants did not allow for an inflation adjusted CT. From a financial perspective, this represents a considerable loss in real value of the grant. As a consequence, the program became less efficient. In addition, it becomes more difficult to argue that the CT accounted for the enrolment of girls. Can really the sum equivalent of a schoolbag explain girls enrolment in school? In addition, the fact that the CT was not adjusted for inflation raises concerns about transparency why did the CTs not take into account the inflation and why should girls who joined the program at a later stage receive less that the girls before them?
